prime.problem: A count table gives every context its own row, and the rows multiply as 27ⁿ. At 3 characters most rows are empty or nearly so, and nothing learned about one row helps any other.
prime.fits: The previous card showed the count table running out of data. This card is the fix Karpathy follows for the rest of the lecture: the one-hot-times-W idea from the bigram course, turned into a small learned table of points shared by every context.
expect: an embedding: a token as a point (a row of C)
one table shared across all context slots
the tanh hidden layer and the softmax output
why nearby points let the model generalize
prime.goal: Draw the Bengio MLP from memory with every shape on it, count its parameters, and explain why learned points generalize to contexts a count table has never seen.

attend: Why does one shared table C for all three context slots need fewer numbers than a table per slot, and what does it assume about position?
Which layer's size grows with the vocabulary, and why does that make it the expensive one?
How can seeing .an during training change the prediction for .on, when the count table can't?
Who decides where a and o sit in space, and what would put them close together?
What does the tanh add that the lookup table alone could not?

must: Count table: one independent row per context → rows grow as 27ⁿ → most rows see few or no examples (71% of 3-char contexts never occur) → no way to share what one row learned with another

Each token becomes a learned point in C → every context goes through the same smooth function of those points → tokens used alike get pushed close together by backprop → evidence about one context transfers to its neighbours, including unseen ones

Parameters scale with vocab × layer width, not with the number of contexts → the output layer (hidden × vocab) dominates: 1,717,000 of 2,236,100 for words, 2,727 of 3,481 for characters → the softmax over the vocabulary is where the cost goes
elevated: C is shared by all 3 slots → the table stays 27 × 2 however long the context → but the slot a token arrived in is kept only by its position in the concatenated x, so W1 must learn a separate block per slot
reference: the paper's letters: y = b + Wx + U tanh(d + Hx), with W (direct connections) set to 0
the paper's column-vector Hx vs Karpathy's row-vector x @ W1 (W1 is H transposed)
Karpathy's walkthrough sizes: 17,000 words, 30 features, 3 context words, 100 hidden units
Table 1 perplexities: 252 (MLP mixed with a trigram), 276 (MLP alone), 312 (best n-gram), 321 (best Kneser-Ney)

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the character-level Bengio model for the row .em → m with every shape on its arrows, then write 3–4 sentences on why it can predict well in a context it has never seen.
checklist: three indices look up rows of one shared C (27 × 2)
the rows are concatenated into 6 numbers, go through tanh(x @ W1 + b1) to 100 units, then h @ W2 + b2 to 27 logits and a softmax
parameter count 54 + 700 + 2,727 = 3,481, most of it in the output layer
C starts random and is trained by backprop with everything else
tokens that behave alike end up nearby, and the network is smooth in its inputs, so learning about one context moves the predictions for similar ones

retrieve.q: Explain what the word "embedding" means in this model, and why the paper calls the representation distributed instead of one row per context.
answer: each token gets a short vector of learned numbers, its row in C
the vector's numbers are shared evidence: any context containing the token uses the same row
a count table stores one independent row per whole context, so nothing is shared

retrieve.q: Walk the row .em → m through the network: which indices go in, what shape comes out of each step, and where does the probability of m appear?
answer: indices 0, 5, 13 look up C[0], C[5], C[13], each (2,)
concatenate to x (6,)
tanh(x @ W1 + b1) gives h (100,)
h @ W2 + b2 gives 27 logits; softmax turns them into 27 probabilities, and entry 13 is P(m)

retrieve.q: You double the vocabulary but keep 30 features and 100 hidden units. Which parameter counts change, roughly by how much, and what does that say about scaling this model to big vocabularies?
answer: C doubles (vocab × 30) and the output layer doubles (100 × vocab + vocab)
the hidden layer does not change (it depends on context × features and hidden size)
the output layer was already about 77% of the model, so cost grows almost linearly with the vocabulary; the paper needed about three weeks on 40 CPUs for 5 epochs of AP News

retrieve.q: Why does a 3-character count table need 531,441 cells while the network needs 3,481 parameters, and what does the network give up in exchange?
answer: the table stores 19,683 contexts × 27 next characters, one number per pair
the network reuses the same 3,481 weights for every context
in exchange it can't memorize each context exactly; it has to generalize through the shared points and may blur rare contexts

compare.q: The bigram network multiplied a one-hot vector by W. How is looking up a row of C the same operation, and what changes when three looked-up rows go through a hidden layer instead of straight to the logits?
answer: one-hot(i) @ C picks row i of C, so the lookup is a linear layer with no bias and no nonlinearity
in the bigram, W is 27 × 27 and each row is directly the logits for one context char
here each row is only 2 numbers and a tanh layer mixes three of them, so the model can combine context and share structure between characters
cost: more to train, and a bad hidden layer can underfit where the bigram table was exact

compare.q: Both models predict the next character from 3 previous ones. Where does each one store what it learned, and how does each fail on a context seen only once?
answer: the count table stores one row of counts per context; the network stores shared weights and points
the table's row for a once-seen context is a single count, so it's all-or-nothing unless smoothed
the network predicts from nearby points, so a rare context borrows from similar ones; it can be wrong when the neighbours behave differently

predict.q: q is rare, and it is almost always followed by u. After training the 2-D model, will q's point sit inside the crowd of common letters or far out on its own? Commit, then check the embeddings-scale-sample card.
predict.answer: Far out. In this course's 2-D run on your M3, q is at (−0.98, +0.19), 0.89 from the centre, the second farthest of all 27 characters. The point for q is set mostly by what tends to follow it, and no other character predicts u so strongly, so nothing pulls it towards the others.

apply.task: By hand, redo the parameter table for Karpathy's final model: 10 numbers per character, 200 hidden units, still 3 characters of context. Count C, the hidden layer (weights + biases) and the output layer separately.
apply.done: Your three counts are 270, 6,200 and 5,427, they add up to 11,897 (what labs/embeddings-scale-sample.py prints for the 10-D model), and you can say which layer is now the largest and why it changed.
apply.hint: The hidden layer's inputs are 3 × 10 = 30. With 200 hidden units and only 27 outputs, the hidden layer (6,200) now outweighs the output layer (5,427): the output is expensive only when the vocabulary is much larger than the hidden size.
